---
title: "Third Down: The Money Down"
subtitle: "The down that decides drives: how far the offense has to go changes everything both sides do, from the routes and the personnel to how many rush, who covers, and who just watches the quarterback."
description: "Third down from both sides of the ball: bucketing third downs (short, medium, long, very long) with league conversion rates by distance and play type; the offense's tools (sticks routes set a yard or two past the line to gain, option routes and other man-beaters, empty formations, third-down protection, and the third-and-long screens and draws that play for field position); the defense's third-down package (dime personnel, pass-rush specialists and stunts) and calls (sticks defense, 2-Man and brackets, simulated pressure and the blitz, Cover 0, rush three/drop eight, the QB spy) with the pre-snap tells for each; why 'past the sticks' matters and when it doesn't; and film-room examples from the Patriots' option routes, Brian Flores's Cover 0, Steve Spagnuolo's third-down pressure and the spies sent after Lamar Jackson."
glossary:
  "Sticks route": "A route whose depth is set by the line to gain, usually so the receiver breaks or settles a yard or two past it, so that a catch at the break is a first down without needing any yards after the catch."
  "Third-down package": "The personnel and calls a team keeps for third down. On defense: extra defensive backs (often dime), pass-rush specialists, and its pressures, disguises and spies. On offense: its best quick concepts and man-beaters, the protections for the opponent's pressures, and the receivers and back it trusts most there."
  "Rush three, drop eight": "A pass defense that sends only three pass rushers and puts eight defenders in coverage, usually on third-and-long, to crowd the throwing windows at and past the line to gain and make the quarterback hold the ball."
  Spy: {def: "A defender (usually a linebacker, safety or nickel back) assigned to the quarterback instead of a receiver or a rush lane: he stays at linebacker depth, keeps his eyes on the quarterback, mirrors his movement and tackles him if he runs or scrambles.", aliases: ["QB spy"]}

`````` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import os
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, style, draw_marker, show_animation, routes as r
from gridiron.play import MARKER_R

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")

PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # the spy: a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
SPLIT = 1.6                # center-to-guard and guard-to-tackle spacing, as in the rest of the book
FIELD_W = 160 / 3


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def oline():
    """The five offensive linemen; only the center is labelled (wide pictures overprint the rest)."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, (i - 2) * SPLIT, "C" if k == "C" else "")
            for i, k in enumerate(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"])]


def spread(rb_w=-1.6):
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2. X and Z on the line, H (slot) and Y (the tight end, flexed out
    like a second slot) a step off it: seven on the line (five linemen, X and Z)."""
    return oline() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, rb_w, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0),
                      O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]


def trips():
    """11 personnel, shotgun 3x1 to the right. X alone on the left, on the line; the tight end Y attached
    to the right tackle, on the line (so he is the end); H and Z off the ball outside him. Numbered from
    the sideline in, #1 is Z, #2 is H, #3 is Y. Seven on the line: five linemen, X and Y."""
    return oline() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8),
                      O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.0), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 16.0)]


def four_down(lde=-5.6, ldt=-0.7, rdt=2.35, rde=5.6):
    """Four defensive linemen: ends outside the tackles, a 1-technique and a 3-technique."""
    return [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, lde, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, ldt, "T"), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, rdt, "T"),
            D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, rde, "E")]


def P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK, fontsize=6.8, ha="center"):
    """A short boxed on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, fontsize=6.8, ha="center", shrink=7):
    """A boxed label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names (both in (d, w))."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = P(fld, p, *text_at), P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=style.INK, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5))


def clean(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where receivers and safeties stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def ruler(fld, play, fs=6.3, upto=40):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) down the left edge of the field window, so the
    faint 5-yard lines read as a scale. Drawn on the Field's ax: gridiron has no ruler."""
    ax = fld.ax
    x_left = FIELD_W - fld.y1 + 0.35
    first = True
    for d in range(5, upto + 1, 5):
        y = play.los + d
        if play.to_go is not None and abs(d - play.to_go) < 1.0:
            continue          # the orange line to gain would run through the label
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if first else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                    ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
            first = False


def timed(p, key, way, kind="path"):
    """Script a player: `way` = [(t, d, w), ...] absolute spots reached at time t (s after the snap).
    Standing still between two times is allowed. (gridiron's actions are speed-based; this turns
    'be here at this moment' into the speed and delay each leg needs.)"""
    cur = np.array(p._cur(key), dtype=float)
    tc, wait = 0.0, 0.0
    for t, d, w in way:
        nxt = np.array([d, w], dtype=float)
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(nxt - cur)))
        if dist < 1e-3:
            wait += t - tc
        else:
            p._add(kind, key, [tuple(cur), tuple(nxt)], speed=dist / (t - tc), delay=wait)
            wait = 0.0
            cur = nxt
        tc = t
    return p


def protect(p, keys=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"), back=1.2):
    """Five linemen set back in pass protection: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in keys:
        p.block(k, pts=[(-back, 0.0)])


# --------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips for print
def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.0, 17.0), width_in=6.5, notes=(), trail_from=None,
             ruler_fs=5.2):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, with faint trails of where he has been (since `trail_from`, if given),
    and the depth ruler down the left edge."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    mv = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in mv if m.side == "off"], [m for m in mv if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in, title=False)
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    clean(ax)
    if ruler_fs:
        ruler(fld, play, fs=ruler_fs, upto=int(window[1]))
    PP = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    start = play._compile()[1] if trail_from is None else trail_from
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.side == "off" and pl.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
            continue
        if t <= start:
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(start, t, 30)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = PP(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
        if pl.side == "off":
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    handed = any(kind == "handoff" and t >= te for kind, _, te in play.ball_events)
    if t <= 0 or handed:            # in the quarterback's hands the ball would hide his label
        bx, by = PP(*play.ball_position(t))
        draw_marker(ax, float(bx) - (0.9 if handed else 0.0), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    for note in notes:              # (text, (d, w)) or (text, (d, w), (d, w) of the player it names)
        text, (d, w) = note[0], note[1]
        x, y = PP(d, w)
        box = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5)
        if len(note) > 2:
            xp, yp = PP(*note[2])
            ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(x), float(y)), fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK,
                        ha="center", va="center", zorder=13, bbox=box,
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=5))
        else:
            ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", zorder=13,
                    bbox=box)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, notes_at=None, ncols=2, width_in=6.5, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.0, 17.0),
          trails_from=None):
    """The print version of an animation: panels at chosen moments of one simulated play.
    `trails_from` = {panel index: time} starts that panel's trails later, so only the late movement shows."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.34)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        snapshot(play, t, ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, notes=(notes_at or {}).get(i, ()),
                 trail_from=(trails_from or {}).get(i))
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6, w_pad=0.4)
    return fig


pct = lambda x, k=0: f"{100 * x:.{k}f}%"      # noqa: E731


def ordinal(n):
    n = int(n)
    if n == 1:
        return "first"
    if n == 2:
        return "second"
    if n == 3:
        return "third"
    return f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"
``````

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (the data behind this chapter's numbers: nflverse via nflreadpy)"}
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

COLS = ["game_id", "play_id", "season", "season_type", "posteam", "defteam", "home_team", "away_team",
        "total_home_score", "total_away_score", "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100", "play_type", "pass",
        "qb_dropback", "qb_scramble", "sack", "qb_kneel", "qb_spike", "third_down_converted", "touchdown", "epa",
        "success", "air_yards", "complete_pass", "receiver_player_name", "rusher_player_name", "rushing_yards",
        "td_team", "penalty", "penalty_team", "penalty_type", "first_down_penalty"]
RAW = pbp(range(2009, 2026), columns=COLS)
PLAYS = RAW[(RAW.season_type == "REG") & RAW.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])
            & (RAW.qb_kneel != 1) & (RAW.qb_spike != 1)].copy()
# a third down is converted if it gains the line to gain (or the offense scores); penalties are left out.
# A touchdown counts only if the offense scored it: a fumble or interception returned for a touchdown is a failure.
PLAYS["conv"] = PLAYS.third_down_converted.eq(1) | (PLAYS.touchdown.eq(1) & PLAYS.td_team.eq(PLAYS.posteam))
T3 = PLAYS[PLAYS.down == 3].copy()

# ---- how often, league-wide, 2016-2025
SR = T3[T3.season >= 2016].groupby("season").conv.mean()
SR_LO, SR_HI = SR.min(), SR.max()
SNAP3 = (PLAYS[PLAYS.season.between(2021, 2025)].down == 3).mean()

# ---- the five seasons the chapter's charts use
R = T3[T3.season.between(2021, 2025)].copy()
R["kind"] = np.where(R.qb_dropback == 1, "drop", "run")
LABS = ["1", "2", "3", "4–6", "7–10", "11+"]
R["b"] = pd.cut(R.ydstogo, [0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 10, 99], labels=LABS)
R["b4"] = pd.cut(R.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 10, 99], labels=["1–3", "4–6", "7–10", "11+"])
BK = R.groupby("b", observed=True).agg(conv=("conv", "mean"), n=("conv", "size"), drop=("qb_dropback", "mean"))
B4 = R.groupby("b4", observed=True).agg(conv=("conv", "mean"), n=("conv", "size"))
B4["share"] = B4.n / B4.n.sum()
CB = R.groupby(["b", "kind"], observed=True).conv.agg(["mean", "size"]).unstack()
EPA_CONV = R.loc[R.conv, "epa"].mean()
EPA_FAIL = R.loc[~R.conv, "epa"].mean()
SWING = EPA_CONV - EPA_FAIL

# ---- past the sticks: aimed passes (no sacks, no scrambles) by where they were thrown
A = R[(R["pass"] == 1) & (R.sack != 1) & (R.qb_scramble != 1) & R.air_yards.notna()].copy()
A["rel"] = A.air_yards - A.ydstogo
REL_LABS = ["10+ short", "6–9 short", "3–5 short", "1–2 short", "at it", "1–2 past", "3–5 past", "6–10 past",
            "11+ past"]
A["rb"] = pd.cut(A.rel, [-99, -10, -6, -3, -1, 0, 2, 5, 10, 99], labels=REL_LABS)
PS = A.groupby("rb", observed=True).agg(n=("conv", "size"), comp=("complete_pass", "mean"), conv=("conv", "mean"))
A["past"] = A.air_yards >= A.ydstogo
PAST_SHARE = A.groupby("b4", observed=True).past.mean()
PAST_CONV = A.groupby(["b4", "past"], observed=True).conv.mean().unstack()
SHORT_COMP = A[(A.complete_pass == 1) & ~A.past].groupby("b", observed=True).conv.mean()

# ---- the defense, from charting (participation: FTN, one source, 2023-2025)
PART = nfl().load_participation(seasons=list(range(2020, 2026))).to_pandas()[
    ["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "defense_personnel", "number_of_pass_rushers", "defense_coverage_type",
     "defense_man_zone_type", "offense_formation"]]
DB3 = PLAYS[(PLAYS.season >= 2020) & (PLAYS.qb_dropback == 1)].merge(
    PART, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")


def n_dbs(s):
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    n = 0
    for part in s.split(","):
        bits = part.strip().split(" ", 1)
        if len(bits) == 2 and bits[0].isdigit() and bits[1] in ("DB", "CB", "FS", "SS", "S"):
            n += int(bits[0])
    return n


DB3["ndb"] = DB3.defense_personnel.map(n_dbs)
DB3["b4"] = pd.cut(DB3.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 10, 99], labels=["1–3", "4–6", "7–10", "11+"])
F = DB3[(DB3.season >= 2023) & (DB3.down == 3)].copy()
lab = F.defense_coverage_type.notna()
mz = F.defense_man_zone_type.isin(["MAN_COVERAGE", "ZONE_COVERAGE"])
DEF = pd.DataFrame({
    "dime": F.groupby("b4", observed=True).ndb.apply(lambda x: (x >= 6).mean()),
    "blitz": F.groupby("b4", observed=True).number_of_pass_rushers.apply(lambda x: (x >= 5).mean()),
    "rush3": F.groupby("b4", observed=True).number_of_pass_rushers.apply(lambda x: (x <= 3).mean()),
    "four": F.groupby("b4", observed=True).number_of_pass_rushers.apply(lambda x: (x == 4).mean()),
    "cov0": F[lab].groupby("b4", observed=True).defense_coverage_type.apply(lambda x: (x == "COVER_0").mean()),
    "man": F[mz].groupby("b4", observed=True).defense_man_zone_type.apply(lambda x: (x == "MAN_COVERAGE").mean()),
})
E12 = DB3[(DB3.season >= 2023) & DB3.down.isin([1, 2])]
DIME_EARLY = (E12.ndb >= 6).mean()
BLITZ_EARLY = (E12.number_of_pass_rushers >= 5).mean()

# outcomes on third-and-7-plus by rushers sent
L = F[F.ydstogo >= 7].copy()
L["rush"] = pd.cut(L.number_of_pass_rushers, [0, 3, 4, 99], labels=["3 or fewer", "4", "5+"])
RO = L.groupby("rush", observed=True).agg(n=("conv", "size"), conv=("conv", "mean"), sack=("sack", "mean"))
R3T = L.groupby(["season", "defteam"]).number_of_pass_rushers.apply(lambda x: (x <= 3).mean())
# the same comparison with the distance held still: third-and-7 to 10 only
RO10 = L[L.ydstogo <= 10].groupby("rush", observed=True).agg(n=("conv", "size"), conv=("conv", "mean"),
                                                              epa=("epa", "mean"), sack=("sack", "mean"))

# 2-Man (two deep safeties, man underneath) by distance, and on early downs
lab_e = DB3[(DB3.season >= 2023) & DB3.down.isin([1, 2]) & DB3.defense_coverage_type.notna()]
TWO_MAN = F[lab].groupby("b4", observed=True).defense_coverage_type.apply(lambda x: (x == "2_MAN").mean())
TWO_MAN_EARLY = (lab_e.defense_coverage_type == "2_MAN").mean()

# empty formations (nobody in the backfield); the formation label exists only through 2022 (NGS charting)
EM = DB3[DB3.season.between(2020, 2022)]
EMPTY_3 = (EM[EM.down == 3].offense_formation == "EMPTY").mean()
EMPTY_E = (EM[EM.down.isin([1, 2])].offense_formation == "EMPTY").mean()

# scrambles on third down, 2021-2025
SCR = R[R.qb_dropback == 1].assign(scr=lambda x: x.qb_scramble == 1)
SCR_SHARE = SCR.scr.mean()
SCR_CONV_LONG = SCR[SCR.scr & SCR.ydstogo.between(7, 10)].conv.mean()
DROP_CONV_LONG = SCR[SCR.ydstogo.between(7, 10)].conv.mean()

# first downs by defensive penalty on third down (every third-down snap, including plays wiped out by a flag)
S3 = RAW[(RAW.season.between(2021, 2025)) & (RAW.season_type == "REG") & (RAW.down == 3)
         & RAW.play_type.isin(["pass", "run", "no_play"]) & (RAW.qb_kneel != 1) & (RAW.qb_spike != 1)].copy()
S3["pen_fd"] = (S3.penalty == 1) & (S3.penalty_team == S3.defteam) & (S3.first_down_penalty == 1)
PEN_FD = S3.pen_fd.mean()
PEN_TOP = S3[S3.pen_fd].penalty_type.value_counts(normalize=True)
# coverage flags (pass interference, holding, illegal contact) against man and zone, charted third-down dropbacks
CF = S3[(S3.season >= 2023) & ((S3.qb_dropback == 1) | (S3.play_type == "no_play"))].merge(
    PART, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
CF = CF[CF.defense_man_zone_type.isin(["MAN_COVERAGE", "ZONE_COVERAGE"])]
CF["flag"] = ((CF.penalty == 1) & (CF.penalty_team == CF.defteam)
              & CF.penalty_type.isin(["Defensive Pass Interference", "Defensive Holding", "Illegal Contact"]))
COV_FLAG = CF.groupby("defense_man_zone_type").flag.mean()

# Cover 0 on third down by defense and season (2020-2022 labels come from NGS, 2023+ from FTN)
C0T = (DB3[(DB3.down == 3) & DB3.defense_coverage_type.notna()]
       .groupby(["season", "defteam"]).defense_coverage_type.apply(lambda x: (x == "COVER_0").mean()))
MIA21_C0, MIA21_RANK = C0T[2021]["MIA"], int(C0T[2021].rank(ascending=False)["MIA"])
MED21_C0 = C0T[2021].median()
MIA20_C0 = C0T[2020]["MIA"]
NE20_C0 = C0T[2020]["NE"]
KC25_C0, KC25_RANK = C0T[2025]["KC"], int(C0T[2025].rank(ascending=False)["KC"])
# ... and on third-and-7 or longer only, where most of the league nearly stops calling it
C07 = (DB3[(DB3.down == 3) & (DB3.ydstogo >= 7) & DB3.defense_coverage_type.notna()]
       .groupby(["season", "defteam"]).defense_coverage_type.apply(lambda x: (x == "COVER_0").mean()))
MIA21_C07, MIA21_C07_RK, MED21_C07 = C07[2021]["MIA"], int(C07[2021].rank(ascending=False)["MIA"]), C07[2021].median()
KC25_C07, KC25_C07_RK, MED25_C07 = C07[2025]["KC"], int(C07[2025].rank(ascending=False)["KC"]), C07[2025].median()

# the Thursday-night game in Miami, November 11, 2021
G = DB3[(DB3.game_id == "2021_10_BAL_MIA") & (DB3.defteam == "MIA")]
G_N, G_C0, G_BL = len(G), int((G.defense_coverage_type == "COVER_0").sum()), (G.number_of_pass_rushers >= 5).mean()
G3 = T3[(T3.game_id == "2021_10_BAL_MIA") & (T3.posteam == "BAL")]
G3_CONV, G3_N = int(G3.conv.sum()), len(G3)
_last = PLAYS[PLAYS.game_id == "2021_10_BAL_MIA"].iloc[-1]
G_HS, G_AS = int(_last.total_home_score), int(_last.total_away_score)      # Miami was the home team

# Spagnuolo's Chiefs: blitz rate (5+ rushers) on early downs and third down
def blitz_rank(season, team="KC"):
    x = DB3[DB3.season == season]
```

Third-and-7, early in the fourth quarter, a three-point game. You can tell it matters before anyone
lines up. The broadcast puts up a graphic of the offense's third-down conversions so far. On the
defensive sideline, two linebackers jog off and two defensive backs jog on, and a pass rusher who has
been standing by the bench all series pulls on his helmet. The offense's best receiver, who stood out
wide on first and second down, now lines up in the slot. The quarterback looks to the sideline, then
points at a safety creeping toward the line and shouts. At the snap that safety drops into the middle
instead of rushing, four defenders rush, the slot receiver pushes eight yards upfield, looks at the
defender in front of him and turns *away* from him toward the sideline, and the ball is already there.
The chains move. Why did half the defense change before the play? What was the quarterback pointing
at? Why eight yards, not seven, and why did the receiver seem to decide where to go after he started
running? And why does the whole stadium seem to agree that this one snap is worth more than the two
before it? This chapter is about **third down**, the down that decides drives, and about why everyone
on the field plays it differently.

**You'll be able to…**

  by a run and by a pass.
- Predict, before the snap, whether the throw will go past the line to gain, and explain when a throw
  short of it is the right call anyway.
- Name the offense's third-down tools (sticks routes, option routes and other man-beaters, empty
  formations, protection, and the screens and draws of third-and-long) and say which distance each is for.
- Use the distance and the defense's personnel to name its most likely call (sticks defense, 2-Man,
  simulated pressure, a blitz, Cover 0, rush three/drop eight, or a spy), spot the few pre-snap tells
  that give a call away, and explain why the rest are disguised.
- Read a conversion chart by distance and play type, and explain why the money down is not quite as
  predictable as it feels.

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles: the linemen (only the center, C, is labelled
on wide pictures), Q the quarterback, R the running back, X and Z the outside receivers, H the slot
receiver and Y the tight end. Defense is outlined orange squares: E and T the defensive ends and
tackles, N a nose tackle, B a stand-up edge player, M the Mike and W the Will linebacker, $ the nickel
back (the slot cornerback), D a dime back (the sixth defensive back), CB the cornerbacks, FS and SS the
free and strong safety. A **green ring** marks the player to watch and a **purple ring** a spy. Blue
arrows are routes, the thick dark-blue arrow a ball carrier's path; solid orange arrows are rushers and
dashed orange arrows zone drops, with the shaded ovals the zones; dotted orange lines join a man-coverage
defender to his receiver. The thick orange line across the field is the **line to gain**, the blue line
the line of scrimmage, and the small numbers on the left edge count yards past the line of scrimmage.
Pictures of a moment in a simulated play show faint lines for where each player has been, and an **×**
where a tackle is made. Left and right are the offense's.

## Why third down is the money down

Start with what third down *is*. On first and second down a bad play is a setback; on third down it is
usually the end of the drive. Convert, and the offense gets three more tries and keeps the ball. Fail,
and outside field-goal range it punts, giving the ball away 40 yards downfield. That cliff is why the
down gets its nickname.

Put a number on the cliff. In the 2021–2025 regular seasons, a converted third down was worth
\+1\.8 expected points to the offense on average, and a failed one
\-1\.3. The difference, about **3\.0 points**, rides on one
snap.[^swing] No other ordinary play swings that much so often: a first-and-10 that gains four yards or
loses one leaves the drive alive either way. Third downs are only about 21% of all runs
and passes, but they decide whether most drives become points or punts.

And the league converts them at a remarkably steady rate: between 39% and
42% in every season from 2016 to 2025, about two in five.[^conv] Rule changes, the
passing boom and the [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) defenses of the last decade have barely
moved it. That stability is a
clue. Third down is a contest both sides prepare for more than any other, and the offense's gains
and the defense's answers have stayed roughly matched.

What makes third down special isn't just the stakes; it's the **information**. On first-and-10 the
defense has to guard against everything, because the offense can do anything. On third-and-8 both
sides know what the offense needs: eight yards, almost certainly through the air. Knowing that, the
defense can specialise. It can take off run defenders and put on pass defenders, take off a big run-stopping
tackle and put on a quick pass rusher, and set every underneath defender's depth by the line to gain.
The offense specialises too: its best receiver moves to where he can get a free release, its routes
are cut to a depth measured from the sticks, and it calls the plays it has practised all week for
exactly this distance. Third down is the down on which the situation tells both teams the most, so it
is the down on which they each carry a separate plan.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game you pick a play from a menu on every down, and the menu looks the same on third-and-8
as on first-and-10. In the NFL, third down has its own section of the call sheet, its own practice day
(in a typical week the third-down plan is installed on Thursday, after the early-down plan;
[The Game Plan](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd)), its own personnel and
often its own play-caller's mindset. The plays on that page are sorted by distance: third-and-1,
third-and-2 to 3, third-and-4 to 6, third-and-7 to 10, third-and-long. A coordinator calling a
third-down play is choosing from a short list built for exactly this distance against exactly this
opponent's third-down habits, not from the whole playbook.
:::

## Four kinds of third down

A broadcaster will tell you "third and short" or "third and long." Coaches cut it finer, because each
distance changes what both sides can do. This book uses four buckets: **short** (1 to 3 yards),
**medium** (4 to 6), **long** (7 to 10) and **very long** (11 or more). Start with how often each kind is
converted, and how.

The chart has two sets of bars, designed runs and dropbacks, at each distance.[^buckets] On
**third-and-1**, runs convert 73% of the time and dropbacks
59%. That isn't because passing is worse; it's because a run needs only a
yard and gets it on a good push, while a pass can go wrong in more ways (a sack, a drop, an incompletion)
that a run can't. By **third-and-3** the two are level, and from **4 yards** on the pass is the only
sensible way: runs on third-and-4 to 6 convert 36%, dropbacks
45%. Offenses know it, which is why they pass on
91% of third-and-4 to 6 snaps and 94%
of third-and-7 to 10.

Each bucket has its own conversion rate and its own logic, and the rest of the chapter follows them
(rates are for 2021–2025).

**Short, 1–3 yards: converted 60%.** A run can get it, so the offense's
whole menu is open and the defense has to defend both. It can't fill the field with defensive backs, it
usually plays tight man coverage because any completion converts, and it often packs the
[box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box). The offense's best weapons are a power run, a quarterback
sneak, or a quick throw that beats tight coverage before the rush arrives. (Third-and-1 and the sneak get
their own chapter, [Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).)

**Medium, 4–6 yards: converted 44%.** The most contested distance. The
offense will almost certainly throw, but it doesn't need to throw far: a 6-yard route run well converts.
The defense plays tight man coverage, mixes in pressure, and leans on mugs and disguise to make the
quarterback guess. It is the bucket of option routes, rubs and mesh on one side and of Cover 1 and
A-gap mugs on the other.

**Long, 7–10 yards: converted 31%.** Almost always a pass, and one that
has to travel past the defenders waiting at the sticks. Now the offense needs a route that takes time to
run, and that time is what the defense attacks: this is where the blitz peaks, because a hot throw to beat
it usually lands short of the line.

**Very long, 11 or more: converted 15%.** The defense can concede anything
short and still win, so it drops more players into coverage, plays deep, and rallies to tackle. Some
offenses take a shot; many take the safe completion, the screen or the draw, and play for a better punt
or a field-goal try.

And the long kinds are common: 46% of third
downs needed 7 yards or more. That is why coaches care so much about first and second down: a four-yard
gain on first down doesn't look like much, but it is the difference between a third down at the top of
that list and one at the bottom ([Early Downs and Field Zones](10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd)).

## The sticks route: a yard past the line

If the target is a known distance, aim past it. That is the whole idea behind a **[sticks
route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sticks-route)**: a route whose depth is set by the line to gain,
usually so the receiver breaks or settles a yard or two beyond it. On first-and-10 a curl might be run
at 12 yards because that's where it fits the defense. On third-and-6 the same receiver runs it at 7 or 8,
because what matters now is that the catch is a first down *at the catch*, with no need for yards after it.
Coaches teach it bluntly: get past the sticks before you break, and don't break short of them.

Why a yard or two past, and not exactly on the line? Two reasons, both about the catch point.

1. **Receivers drift back toward the ball.** A receiver who breaks at 7 and turns back to the
   quarterback is caught at 6 and a half, short of a third-and-7. A route designed at 8 leaves room for
   that.
2. **Defenders sit on the sticks.** On third down the underneath defenders' landmark *is* the line to
   gain (more below). A ball caught right on the line is caught in front of a defender who is already
   there and only has to tackle forward.

But a sticks route can't go *too* far past the line, because every extra yard of depth costs completion
probability: it takes the receiver longer to get there, and the quarterback has to hold the ball against
the rush. The design problem of third-and-medium is to get a receiver open as close past the sticks as
possible, as fast as possible. Against the man coverage defenses favour at those distances, that means
beating a defender who knows where you're going.

### The answer to man: routes that choose

Here is a typical third-and-7 against Cover 1. The offense is in trips to the right; the defense plays
man coverage with one deep safety and a robber. (Staffs call that low middle player a **robber**, a
[**rat**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rat) or a **hole** player depending on the playbook and how deep he sits;
[Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd) draws the versions.)

The option route is the heart of it ([Passing Game Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)
taught the rule). A man defender has to line up on one side of his receiver, and that side, his
[leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside), is the side he is protecting. Here the
nickel sits inside H, taking away the quickest throws, the slant and the in-cut toward the middle. So H
pushes to 8 yards, past the line, and breaks the other way, toward the sideline, where the nickel can't get
to him in time and the robber can't help.

That inside alignment is a choice, not the default. With a robber in the middle, many defenses play the
slot defender *outside* and funnel the receiver inside to the help; this one is taking away the quick
slant instead. Against that outside alignment the rule sends H inside, straight toward the robber, and the
quarterback has to see it and look elsewhere. And the rule has a third branch that coaches always teach:
if the defender is soft, head-up, or dropping into a zone, **sit it down** in the open space past the
sticks, face the quarterback and catch the ball. That is why the quarterback reads two things, not one: the
nickel's leverage and where the robber is standing. The receiver doesn't guess; he reads, and the
quarterback reads with him, which is why option routes go to the receivers a quarterback trusts most.

The rest of the concept exists to protect that one decision. The two go routes outside are
*clear-outs*: they take the cornerbacks, who are in man coverage and must run with them, out of the area
where H will break. Y's seam up the middle gives the single deep safety something to worry about, so he
can't drift toward the sideline to help on H. And the back is the checkdown. If the defense blitzes, he
blocks; if it doesn't, he is the safe throw, short of the sticks, for when the option route is covered.

The option route is one of a family of third-down man-beaters, all of which do the same job by
different means: give the receiver an advantage over a defender who has no help.

- **Rubs and bunches.** Line receivers up close together, a [bunch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bunch),
  and send them across each other's paths. Each man defender has to fight through traffic to follow his
  receiver, while zone defenders would just swap receivers. ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)
  draws the concepts; where a rub becomes illegal offensive pass interference is in
  [Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).)
- **Mesh.** Two shallow crossers who brush past each other in the middle
  ([mesh](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh)), with the same traffic problem for their defenders; the
  crossers usually settle a few yards past a third-and-medium line to gain.
- **Slants and quick outs.** The fastest throws on the field, aimed at the receiver who has the
  leverage he wants before the snap. They beat a blitz too, because the ball is out before the rush
  arrives.
- **Matchups.** The offense moves its best receiver to wherever the defense's worst cover man will
  have to take him, usually the slot, against a linebacker or a safety. On third down, *who* covers whom
  often matters more than the concept, which is why defenses answer the best receiver with a
  [bracket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bracket): two defenders on him, one under and one over, or one
  inside and one outside. "Take away their guy and make somebody else beat us" is a third-down plan in
  itself.
- **Empty.** Five receivers spread across the field and nobody in the backfield
  ([empty](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-empty)). It thins the box, forces the defense to show man or zone
  by how it lines up, and usually leaves a linebacker on a receiver. Offenses lined up in empty on
  19% of third-down dropbacks in 2020–2022, against 12% on first and
  second down.[^empty] The price is protection: with no back to block, a sixth rusher is the quarterback's
  problem, and he has to throw hot.

Why does all this aim at man coverage? Because that is what defenses play on third-and-short and
medium. In 2023–2025, charted third-down dropbacks at 1 to 3 yards to go were played in man coverage
58% of the time, and at 4 to 6 yards 58%;
at 11 or more it fell to 26%.[^defdata] A zone defense on
third-and-4 has defenders spread across the field waiting for the ball, and any route that finds the
space between two of them, five yards deep, converts. Man coverage takes that space away by putting a
defender on every receiver. The offense's reply is to make that defender's life as hard as possible
for about a second and a half.

Man coverage has one more price on third down: **flags**. A man defender is attached to his receiver, and
when he is beaten his last resort is a grab. On charted third-down dropbacks in 2023–2025, defenders were
flagged for [pass interference](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-pass-interference),
[defensive holding](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-holding) or illegal contact on
4\.8% of snaps in man coverage, against
1\.6% in zone, about three times as often. All three give the offense
an automatic first down whatever the distance. Across 2021–2025, about one third-down snap in 25
(4\.0%) ended in a first down by defensive penalty, pass interference and holding the
most common.[^flags] The conversion rates in this chapter leave those out, so they slightly understate how
often drives survive third down, and every one of those flags is a quiet cost of playing man.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The sticks route exists because on third down the distance is fixed in advance, so the offense can aim
at one yard and give the receiver the right to choose his break. **What it gives up:** a route set to the
sticks hands the defense a target depth too, and the two sides have been trading moves over that yard
ever since. Defenders learn to sit at the sticks and drive on the break; receivers answer by selling the
sit and turning upfield (a "stick-nod"), quarterbacks by throwing to the back shoulder, away from the
defender's drive. Defenses answer with man coverage from depth and safeties over the top, so that the
receiver who turns upfield runs into help; offenses answer that with rubs. That steady trading of moves
is why the league's third-down rate barely moves.
:::

## Past the sticks: what the numbers say, and when it doesn't matter

Every broadcaster has said it: "you have to throw it past the sticks on third down." Here is how true
that is.

The shape of the bars is the case for the sticks route.[^sticksdata] Throws aimed 10 or more yards short
of the line to gain were completed 77% of the time and converted
only 9%. Throws aimed one or two yards past it converted
63%, the best of any group. Past the line, the bar and the line meet:
every completion there converts, so conversion simply tracks completion rate, and falls as the throws get
deeper and harder to complete. Notice
the dip for throws aimed right **at** the line (52%, with completions
falling off too): that is very likely, at least in part, the sticks-sitting defender at work, and it is the
reason the sticks route is set a yard or two beyond.

So the broadcasters are mostly right. But "past the sticks" is a rule about *averages*, and there are
four situations in which a throw short of the line is the right one.

1. **Third-and-short.** Even a catch behind the line can convert when the line is only a yard or two
   away. Completed throws short of the sticks converted 80% of the time on
   third-and-1 and 69% on third-and-2, against 36%
   on third-and-7 to 10 and 11% on 11 or more. On third-and-1 a pass to
   the flat, caught a yard *behind* the line with nobody near the receiver, is a good play; it's a run
   with a better start.
2. **The receiver who will run after the catch.** Screens and quick throws to the offense's best
   open-field runner are short by design: the bet is on the yards after the catch, and against a defense
   playing deep it can be a good bet.
3. **Four-down territory.** When an offense near midfield has already decided it will go for it on
   fourth down if it needs to, third-and-6 is really "third-and-6 with two tries." A five-yard completion
   that sets up fourth-and-1 is then a fine outcome
   ([Early Downs and Field Zones](10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd) has the field zones;
   [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) the decision).
4. **Field-goal range and field position.** On third-and-12 at the opponent's 35, a 7-yard completion
   doesn't convert, but it turns a 52-yard field-goal try into a 45-yard one. Deep in his own end, an
   offense facing third-and-15 may simply want a safe gain and a punt from further out.

How often do offenses throw past the line? It depends heavily on the distance:
78% of aimed passes on third-and-1 to 3 were thrown at or past it,
68% at 4 to 6, 52% at 7 to 10 and only
29% at 11 or more. The longer the distance, the more the defense can make
the deep throw hard and the short throw easy, and the more often the quarterback takes the short one.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A completion short of the sticks on third down is a quarterback mistake." Sometimes. But on
third-and-11 or more the defense's whole design is to make the short completion the only open one, with
everybody else deep and waiting at the line to gain. A quarterback who forces the ball into that coverage
risks an interception to chase a first down that converts less than one time in five even when
everything goes right. Taking the checkdown, getting five yards, and punting from further out is often
the better play. The mistake is the *other* one: the third-and-5 checkdown that gets four, when a
receiver was open at six.
:::

## Third-and-long: screens, draws and the punt

On third-and-12 the odds are poor whatever the offense calls: dropbacks converted
16% of third-and-11-or-more snaps in 2021–2025. Here a lot of
offenses stop trying to win the down outright and start trying to win the *possession*: to avoid the
sack, the interception and the holding penalty, and to make the punt that follows a little shorter. Two
plays do most of that work, and both turn the defense's third-and-long plan against it.

The **screen** lets the pass rush through and throws behind it. On third-and-long the defense's
rushers are going all-out for the quarterback and its coverage players are deep and facing the quarterback, so a
back or receiver who catches the ball behind the line with linemen in front of him has room. The
**draw** shows a pass, then hands the ball off up the middle, into the space the linebackers just left
by dropping into coverage. Its mechanics, and Paul Brown's Browns who made it famous, are in
[Gap Schemes](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd). Here is why it lives on third down.

::: {#cell-fig-draw-vs-dime .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def draw_play():
    dfn = four_down(ldt=-2.35, rdt=2.35) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.6, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.5, "D"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 14.0, 8.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=12)
    # receivers sell the pass: verticals that pull the defensive backs away
    p.route("X", r.go(16.5)); p.route("Z", r.go(16.5)); p.route("H", r.seam(15)); p.route("Y", r.seam(15))
    # quarterback: a short drop as if to throw; the handoff comes at 0.9 s
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.6, -6.5, 0.0), (1.2, -6.5, 0.0)], "qbdrop")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.55, -5.0, -1.6), (0.9, -5.6, -0.6), (1.5, -2.5, 0.3), (2.1, 1.5, 1.1),
                    (2.7, 6.0, 2.2), (3.3, 9.4, 2.5)], "run")
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.9)
    # line: pass sets, then each guard rides his tackle out and upfield from the inside shoulder;
    # the uncovered center climbs to the Mike and stays on him
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.6, -2.4, -4.6), (1.6, -3.4, -5.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.6, -1.5, -1.9), (1.6, -2.0, -2.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.8, -0.2, 0.2), (2.2, 4.6, 0.4), (3.3, 5.0, 0.5)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.6, -1.5, 1.9), (1.6, -2.0, 2.3)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.6, -2.4, 4.6), (1.6, -3.4, 5.8)], "block")
    timed(p, "LDE", [(0.6, -1.6, -6.4), (1.6, -3.6, -6.8)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.6, -0.8, -2.6), (1.6, -1.8, -3.2)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.6, -0.8, 2.6), (1.6, -1.8, 3.2)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDE", [(0.6, -1.6, 6.4), (1.6, -3.6, 6.8)], "rush")
    # the defense drops for the pass, then has to come back; the Mike is met by the center
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(0.9, 10.0, 0.4), (1.6, 10.0, 0.4), (2.3, 5.8, 0.4), (3.3, 5.8, 0.4)], "drop")
    timed(p, "NB", [(1.2, 10.5, -11.0), (2.0, 12.5, -10.5), (3.3, 10.2, 1.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "DB", [(1.2, 10.5, 11.0), (2.0, 12.5, 10.5), (3.3, 11.6, 4.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.2, 17.0, -8.5), (2.0, 17.0, -8.0), (3.3, 12.4, 0.9)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.2, 17.0, 8.5), (2.0, 17.0, 8.0), (3.3, 10.6, 3.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.6, 15.0, -15.8)], "drop"); timed(p, "RCB", [(1.6, 15.0, 15.8)], "drop")
    p.highlight("RB")
    return p
```

A third-and-12 draw against a dime defense (simulated, illustrative). Snap: the defense has four rushers (both tackles lined up outside the guards, so nobody is over the center), one linebacker (M) and six defensive backs, two of them deep. +0.8 s: everything says pass. The quarterback has dropped, the linemen have set back as if to pass-block and let the rushers come upfield, the receivers are running deep, and the defense is dropping into coverage. +1.7 s: the back takes the handoff and heads up the middle, where the Mike was standing before he bailed to 10 yards; the guards ride the tackles outward, and the center, with nobody over him, climbs to the Mike. +3.3 s: the back has cut off the center's block on the Mike and reached the defensive backs, who rallied down from the sticks (their trails from 2.4 s shown) and tackle him at about 9.5 yards, short of the line to gain (orange). The draw worked as designed and still didn't convert: that is the bargain.
:::
:::


Watch what the defense's third-and-long plan does to itself. It has taken off a linebacker for a sixth
defensive back, so there is one fewer big body near the line. Its remaining linebacker drops to 10 yards
at the snap, because that is where the passing windows are. Its rushers come upfield as fast as they can,
because they are trying to reach a quarterback who is about to throw. The draw uses all three: the
linemen let the rushers run themselves past the play, and the back runs into the space the dropping
linebacker left. Against a defense playing the pass, it's one of the few runs with numbers on its side.

And it still usually fails to convert. Designed runs on third-and-11 or more converted only
5% of the time in 2021–2025, because the defensive backs who dropped
to the sticks are waiting there to tackle. So why call it? Partly because a 9-yard run on third-and-12 is
a better outcome than a sack, an interception or an incompletion, especially near midfield, where it
improves the punt or sets up a long field-goal try. Partly to protect the next third down: a defense that
has been gashed by a draw rushes a half-step more carefully the next time, and its linebacker drops a
half-step later. That is a [constraint play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-constraint-play), a call
that exists to keep the defense honest against another ([Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)).

The same logic explains the third-and-long screen, which also rarely converts but pays in the same
currency. Both are cheap ways to lose the down safely, with a small chance of winning
it big against a defense that guessed wrong.

## The defense's third-down package

When the defense knows the offense will throw, it changes the people on the field. That is a
**[third-down package](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-third-down-package)**: the personnel and calls
a team keeps for third down. On defense it means more defensive backs, faster pass rushers, and the
pressures and disguises it has practised all week. On offense it means its best quick concepts, its
protections for the opponent's pressures, and the receivers and back it trusts most on the money down.

The defensive half is visible from your couch, and the data show it clearly.

::: {#cell-fig-defense-by-distance .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}

          ("blitz", "Blitz (5+ rushers)", style.SERIES[1], "s", "-"),

            fontweight="bold")
```

**Personnel.** Defenses had six or more defensive backs on the field for
11% of third-and-short dropbacks, 42%
at 7 to 10 yards and 45% at 11 or more, against
8% on first and second down.[^defdata2] The dime back replaces a linebacker: he
covers better and tackles worse, and on a down when the offense is very likely to throw that is a good
trade. It is also a bet, and the draw above is how the offense makes the defense pay when the bet is wrong.

**Pass rushers.** The same logic applies up front. A 330-pound run-stopping tackle who is excellent on
first-and-10 is wasted on third-and-9, so many defenses replace him with a lighter, quicker rusher, or put
four edge rushers on the field together, with two of them lined up inside over the guards. Steve
Spagnuolo's 2007 Giants had a package of four pass rushers that *Sports Illustrated* later called his
"Four Aces"; by 2011 the Giants' version, four defensive ends on third-and-long, was known as their
"NASCAR" package, for its speed.[^nascar] Most NFL defenses now have some version of it, and many rosters
carry a rusher or two who play mostly on passing downs. And the most common third-down "pressure" is not a
blitz at all: it is four rushers running a [stunt](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stunt), an end and a
tackle crossing paths so that one of them comes free through a gap the protection thought was covered
([The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd)). A front of four quick rushers is built for exactly
that.

**Calls.** Third down is also where a defense spends the calls it has been saving. The chart shows their
shape by distance; the rest of this chapter takes the families in turn: sitting at the sticks, 2-Man,
pressure, Cover 0, rushing three, and spying the quarterback.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: the third-down back, Patriots 2018–2019"}
The offensive half of the package has faces too. Under Bill Belichick and Josh McDaniels the Patriots
kept a running back whose main job was third down: first picking up blitzers in pass protection, then
catching passes and running the option routes out of the backfield that linebackers struggle to cover. James White was New England's
most-targeted receiver on third down in both 2018 and 2019, the target on
26% of Tom Brady's third-down throws to a named receiver across the two seasons.[^pats]
**What to notice:** on third down, watch which back comes into the game. If it isn't the starter, the
substitution is a statement: protection and routes, not runs.
:::

## Sticks defense: keep it in front

The simplest third-down defense is the one that makes the offense's own target its landmark. If the
offense needs 12 yards, the defense can give up 11. Coaches call it playing the sticks: zone defenders
drop to (or just past) the line to gain, keep every receiver in front of them, and tackle the catch
short of it.

::: {#cell-fig-sticks-defense .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def c3_def(to_go, under_d, cb_drop, cb_d, fs_d, fs_drop):
    dfn = four_down() + [
        D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.2, "M"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -10.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 10.0, "SS"),
        D("LCB", "CB", cb_d, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", cb_d, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", fs_d, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=to_go)
    for k in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)])
    zs = (6.0, 8.0) if under_d < 9 else (5.0, 8.0)
    p.drop("NB", (under_d, -11.5), zone=zs); p.drop("WILL", (under_d, -4.5), zone=zs)
    p.drop("MIKE", (under_d, 4.5), zone=zs); p.drop("SS", (under_d, 11.5), zone=zs)
    p.drop("LCB", (cb_drop, -15.5), zone=(8.0, 9.5)); p.drop("RCB", (cb_drop, 15.5), zone=(8.0, 9.5))
    p.drop("FS", (fs_drop, 0.0), zone=(8.0, 12.0))
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
for ax, (tg, ud, cbx, cbd, fsd, fsx, title) in zip(axes, [
        (4, 6.0, 14.0, 5.5, 11.0, 15.0, "3rd & 4: underneath squeezes to 6"),
        (12, 12.5, 18.5, 8.0, 15.5, 20.5, "3rd & 12: underneath sinks to the sticks")]):
    p = c3_def(tg, ud, cbx, cbd, fsd, fsx)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 27.0), title=False, width_in=3.2)
    clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=7.8, loc="left", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Why does this work? Because the offense's routes have to be *finished* to be useful. A curl at 14 yards
takes about two seconds to run; a defender who starts at 12 and only has to take one step and tackle has
almost no ground to cover. And the defense doesn't need to stop the catch, only the extra yard. This is
very likely part of the reason for the dip in the past-the-sticks chart at throws aimed right at the line:
the defender standing on the line to gain catches the receiver there.

What does it give up? **Everything short.** A sticks defense on third-and-12 hands the offense an open
6-yard route on almost every snap, which is fine until the offense is in four-down territory and happy to
take it, or has a receiver who can make a man miss. It also gives the quarterback **time**, because the
underneath defenders are reading him rather than rushing him. And it asks for good **tackling**: a defense
that misses the first tackle at the sticks has turned a stop into a first down. The cure for the short
completion is a fast defense that rallies to it; for the time, mixing in pressure; for the tackling, there
is no scheme.

### Man under, two deep: 2-Man

Zone at the sticks has a cousin built on man coverage. In
**[2-Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-man)** (also called Cover 5), two safeties split the deep field
in halves and the five defenders underneath play man, usually in
[trail technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trail-technique): a step behind the receiver and on his
inside hip, daring him to run past, because a safety is waiting over the top. It is the classic
third-and-medium-to-long man call against option-route offenses. The underneath defender can sit on the
short break, the sticks route, with no fear of the deep ball, and the receiver who turns upfield runs into
a safety. Defenses played it on 8% to 9% of charted
third-and-4-to-10 dropbacks in 2023–2025, against 5% on early downs.[^twoman]

The price is the rush and the middle. Two deep and five in man leaves four rushers and nobody to spy or rob,
so a quarterback who escapes the pocket has open grass in front of him: the man defenders are running with
their receivers, backs turned. That is why 2-Man is a favourite against pocket passers and a risk against
quarterbacks who run (the spy, below, is the answer to that). The pre-snap tell is two high safeties with the
cornerbacks and the nickel tight and *inside* their receivers; the trap is that the same picture can turn into
a two-deep zone at the snap.

## Pressure on third down: simulated pressure and the blitz

The second family is pressure. [Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)
built the tools; here is why third down is where they live.

On third down the quarterback has to hold the ball until a route past the sticks is open, so every
fraction of a second the defense takes away is worth more than on any other down. Pressure that forces
the ball out early forces it out *short*, usually to a hot receiver in front of the line to gain, and on
third-and-8 a hot throw that gains five is a defensive win.

That is why the blitz peaks at **third-and-7 to 10**. In 2023–2025 defenses sent five or more rushers on
38% of third-and-7 to 10 dropbacks, against 25%
on first and second down. At that distance the hot throw is short of the sticks, so the defense can live
with it; the routes that convert take time to develop, so pressure can kill them. At **11 or more** the
blitz rate falls to 17%: the defense doesn't need to force the ball out,
because a short throw already loses. At **4 to 6**, blitzing is more dangerous, because the hot throw can
convert, so blitz rates there are lower, and most defenses that do blitz play man coverage behind it, not
zone (the third-down chart in
[Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd) counts it).

**Simulated pressure** fits third down even better. It shows a blitz, gets the protection to commit and
the quarterback to plan a hot throw, then rushes four from unexpected places and drops seven, often with a
lineman sitting in exactly the short window the hot throw was aimed at. On third-and-long the quarterback
who throws hot into that window gains nothing, and the one who waits for a route past the sticks is facing
a rusher his protection didn't count. To see why "didn't count" matters, look at the other side of the ball.

### The offense's answer: count, slide, keep the back in

Remember the quarterback in the opening, pointing at a safety and shouting. He was **counting**. Before
every third-down snap the offense names the defenders it thinks can rush, picks one as the reference point
(the [Mike identification](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-identification)), and every blocker
counts his man from him, so all of them block the same picture ([Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)).
On third down that call does most of the work:

- **Slide toward the threat.** The line [slides](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection) toward
  the side the extra rusher is most likely to come from, blocking gaps rather than men, so a stunt or a
  late blitzer runs into a blocker.
- **Six-man protection.** The back stays in to take the first extra rusher (the
  [half-slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-half-slide) is the everyday version), which answers a
  five-man pressure with six blockers. The cost is one fewer receiver, on the down when the offense most
  needs a man open.
- **Hot and sight adjust.** When the defense brings more than the protection can block, the quarterback
  throws [hot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) to the receiver whose defender just blitzed, and a
  receiver who sees the same blitz may cut his route short
  ([sight adjust](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sight-adjust)). That is the defense's bet: the hot throw
  is fast, and on third-and-8 it is usually short.

So when a simulated pressure walks a safety down and then drops him, it isn't just "showing blitz." It is
attacking the count: the protection slid toward the safety, the back was told to check him, and the
fourth rusher comes from the other side, where the count left a gap. Simulated pressures are designed to
beat the protection's counting rules ("who's the fifth?"), and that is why third down is where they live.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs 2024 — Spagnuolo saves it for third down"}
Steve Spagnuolo, the Chiefs' defensive coordinator since 2019 (and still in 2026), is the clearest modern
case of a coordinator whose pressure is *situational*. In 2024 the Chiefs sent five or more rushers on
32% of first- and second-down dropbacks, already above the league's typical rate
(median 23%); on third down it was 42%, the second-highest rate in the
NFL (league median 28%). In 2025 the pattern held: 32% early,
37% on third down. The 2025 Chiefs also played Cover 0 on 11\.2% of
their charted third-down dropbacks, the most in the league.[^kc] The two calls go together: the all-out
blitz with no deep safety, kept for third down, when a hot throw that doesn't get to the line ends the drive.

**What to notice:** on a Chiefs third down, count the defenders within five yards of the line before the
snap, then count again after it. Spagnuolo's famous calls are the six-man zeros
([Blitzing](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) breaks down the ones from Super Bowl LVIII),
but most of his third downs show that look and bring four or five.

**And the honest footnote:** pressure is a bet, not a guarantee. The 2024 Chiefs allowed third-down
conversions on 43% of opponents' third downs, only the
24th-best rate in the league, in a 15–2 season. A blitz that gets home ends the drive;
one that doesn't leaves a receiver alone.
:::

## Cover 0: all in

The most aggressive third-down call is **Cover 0**: man coverage on every eligible receiver, nobody deep,
and everyone else rushing. [Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd) and
[Blitzing](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) drew it; this section is about *when*.

Across the league it is above all a **short-yardage** call. On third-and-1 to 3, Cover 0 was played on
9% of charted dropbacks in 2023–2025; on third-and-11 or more,
2%. Why short? Two reasons.

1. **A completion costs less.** With nobody deep, any completion that beats its man can go a long way. But
   on third-and-2 the defense loses the down on almost any completion anyway, so the bet risks less than on
   third-and-10, where a short completion is still a stop and the defense would be giving up its safe
   outcome to gamble.
2. **Every defender is close to the line, which helps against the run.** On third-and-short the offense
   might run; Cover 0 puts eight or nine defenders within a few yards of the ball.

Some coordinators use it at longer distances too, for a third reason: **it forces the decision now.** A
quarterback facing six rushers and no safety has well under two seconds. He must throw hot, against tight
man coverage, before the route has developed. On third-and-2 that hot throw can convert, but on
third-and-6 or 7 the routes fast enough to beat the rush mostly end short of the line. That is the Cover 0
of the film rooms below. Spagnuolo's Chiefs and Flores's Dolphins called it on short third downs like
everyone else, but kept calling it on long ones, where most of the league nearly stops: on third-and-7 or
longer, the 2021 Dolphins played Cover 0 on 24% of charted dropbacks
(first in the NFL; league median 3%), and the 2025 Chiefs on
10% (second; median 2%).[^c0long] They were
betting that the hot throw would land short. The league habit (short yardage, for the run and because the
completion converts anyway) and theirs (medium and long, because the completion lands short) are two
answers to the same question: where is the quick completion least damaging?

What it gives up is everything behind it. A Cover 0 blitz that doesn't get home is one broken tackle away
from a touchdown, and offenses that see it coming (both safeties walking down, corners pressed, linebackers
mugged in the A gaps) answer with slants, rubs, and protection that keeps an extra blocker in.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Dolphins 2021 — Brian Flores's third-down zeros"}
Brian Flores spent fifteen seasons in Bill Belichick's New England organisation (four in scouting, then
eleven on the coaching staff) before becoming Miami's head coach (2019–2021), and his Dolphins played Cover 0 more than anyone. In 2020 they played it on
17% of charted third-down dropbacks, level with Belichick's Patriots
(17%) at the top of the league; in 2021 on 28%, the most in the NFL
and more than four times the league median (7%).[^mia]

The signature night came on Thursday, November 11, 2021, when the 2–7 Dolphins beat the 6–2 Ravens
22–10 in Miami. Flores sent five or more rushers on
52% of Lamar Jackson's 48 charted dropbacks and played Cover 0 on
17 of them, with his safeties walked up as rushers or man defenders, and Baltimore converted
2 of 14 third downs. The Ravens' own columnist described an offense
"overwhelmed by relentless blitzes."[^eisenberg]

**What to notice:** before the snap, count the deep safeties. If there are none, and the corners are
pressed, it is Cover 0 or a disguise of it, and the ball has to come out in well under two seconds. Flores kept
the same idea in Minnesota (he has been the Vikings' defensive coordinator since 2023, and still is in
2026), where the Cover 0 look is as often a disguise as a call.
:::

## Rush three, drop eight

At the other end of the dial is a call that sounds like giving up: **[rush three, drop
eight](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rush-three-drop-eight)**. Three rushers, eight defenders in
coverage, usually on third-and-long.

::: {#cell-fig-rush-three .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def rush3_play():
    dfn = [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "E"),
           D("OLB", "OLB", 1.0, -6.6, "B"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.5, 0.8, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.5, "D"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 6.0, "SS"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 15.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=12)
    for k in ("LDE", "NT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-2.0, 0.0)])
    # protection: tackles on the ends, center and left guard double the nose, right guard looks for work
    p.block("LT", pts=[(-1.3, -0.5)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(-1.3, 0.5)])
    p.block("LG", pts=[(-0.8, 0.8)]); p.block("C", pts=[(-0.7, 0.0)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(-1.2, 0.9)])
    p.route("X", r.curl(13.5)); p.route("Z", r.curl(13.5))
    p.route("H", r.dig(14.5, 8)); p.route("Y", r.seam(17))
    p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (2.5, 3.4), (8.0, 3.7)], side=-1)       # check, then release past the line
    zs = (5.0, 7.5)
    p.drop("NB", (12.0, -13.0), zone=zs); p.drop("OLB", (11.5, -6.0), zone=zs); p.drop("MIKE", (13.0, 0.0), zone=zs)
    p.drop("SS", (11.5, 6.0), zone=zs); p.drop("DB", (12.0, 13.0), zone=zs)
    p.drop("LCB", (18.5, -16.0), zone=(7.0, 11.0)); p.drop("RCB", (18.5, 16.0), zone=(7.0, 11.0))
    p.drop("FS", (21.0, 0.0), zone=(7.0, 12.0))
    return p


p = rush3_play()
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 27.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, 24.7, -11.0, "five underneath at 11–13 yards:\nevery window at the sticks is filled", fontsize=6.5)
say(fld, p, 24.7, 12.0, "three deep at 18–21 yards:\nnothing gets over the top", fontsize=6.5)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.8, 10.5), (-1.9, 2.5), "three rushers, five blockers: C and LG\ndouble the nose, RG looks for work")
point_to(fld, p, (-4.6, -13.5), (3.0, -5.3), "checkdown: open,\nabout 10 yards short")
plt.show()
```

Behind them, five underneath defenders sink to 11 to 13 yards, right on the line to gain (orange), and three deep defenders sit at 18 to 21 yards. The offense runs a typical third-and-long pattern: curls at the sticks outside, a dig at 13 from the left slot, and the tight end up the seam to hold the deep middle. Every one of those windows has a defender in it. The offense has five blockers for three rushers, so the center and left guard double the nose and the right guard looks for work, and the back's checkdown is wide open, about 10 yards short.](10-02-third-down_files/figure-html/fig-rush-three-output-1.svg){#fig-rush-three}
:::
:::


The logic is the sticks defense taken to its limit. On third-and-12 the offense needs a completion past
12 yards, and eight defenders can put a body in every window at that depth and still keep three deep. The
quarterback is offered the checkdown and little else.

The price is **time**. Three rushers against five blockers will rarely get home quickly: the offense has
two spare linemen to double-team the best rusher, and the quarterback can hold the ball for four seconds
or more. Given that long, receivers can run a second route, and a quarterback who can move will find the
gaps in the rush and scramble through them. That is why rush-three calls often come with the next section's
idea attached, a defender assigned to the quarterback, and why defenses mix them with pressure: a quarterback
who sees three rushers on one third-and-long can't assume he'll get time on the next.

How rare is it, and does it work? Across 2023–2025 defenses rushed three or fewer on
8% of third-and-11-or-more dropbacks and 4%
at 7 to 10. On third-and-7 or longer, offenses converted 21% against
three or fewer rushers, 24% against four and 31%
against five or more.[^rush3] Sack rates run the way you'd expect:
7\.7% with three rushers, 12\.4% with
five or more.

Read those conversion rates carefully, because they seem to say the blitz is the *worst* call on
third-and-long. Most of that is the distance hiding inside the average. Three-man rushes come mostly on the
very longest downs, which are the hardest to convert whatever the defense does, and blitzes mostly at 7 to
10, which are easier. Hold the distance still and the gap nearly closes: on third-and-7 to 10 alone,
offenses converted 31% against four rushers and
34% against five or more. So the blitz doesn't stop third-and-long more
often than a four-man rush, on average. It does change *how* the down ends: more sacks, more hurried throws,
and the occasional receiver left alone. That near-tie is roughly what you'd expect if coordinators are
mixing their calls well. If one call were clearly better, everyone would call it more, offenses would
prepare for it, and its edge would shrink. The blitz earns its place by being one option in a mix the
quarterback can't predict, not by winning every time it is called.

Some defenses lean on it. Brian Flores's 2023 Vikings, the league's heaviest blitzers that season, also
rushed three or fewer on 30% of their third-and-7-or-longer dropbacks, the most in the
NFL: a defense that might send seven or three, from the same look. In 2025 the leaders were Jesse Minter's
Chargers (19%; Minter is the Ravens' head coach in 2026) and Kelvin Sheppard's
Lions (18%).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: rush three, drop eight"}
**What it solves:** on third-and-long the offense needs a completion past the sticks, so the defense puts
its numbers where the completion has to happen, and accepts a free short throw. **What it gives up:** the
pass rush. With only three rushing, the quarterback gets time, and time eventually beats any coverage. It
works best against quarterbacks who don't run and offenses without a receiver who can turn a checkdown into
twelve yards, and it works only as one call in a mix.
:::

## The spy

The last family answers a problem that third down's own calls create. Drop eight into coverage, or even
seven, and the coverage covers everyone *except* the man with the ball. Play man coverage, and it is
worse: every man defender is running with his receiver, **back turned to the quarterback**, so nobody sees
him take off. (Zone defenders at least face the quarterback and can come up when he runs.) A quarterback
who can run looks downfield, sees every receiver covered, sees the rush lanes open, and goes. Scrambles
were only 6% of third-down dropbacks in 2021–2025, but on third-and-7 to 10 they
converted 48% of the time, against 32% for dropbacks as a
whole.[^scramble] Against the quarterbacks who scramble most, that is a weapon a defense has to plan for.

The defense's answer is the **[spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy)** (or **[QB
spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-spy)**): a defender assigned not to a receiver or a rush lane but to
the quarterback himself. He stands at linebacker depth, usually 5 to 7 yards off the ball and in front of
the quarterback, keeps his eyes on him, and mirrors him. If the quarterback throws, the spy has done
nothing, which is the price. If he runs, the spy meets him.

::: {#cell-fig-spy .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def spy_play():
    dfn = four_down(lde=-6.4, rde=6.4) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -5.5, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 9.5, "SS"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
    # routes: outs set a yard and a half past a third-and-6 line (offsets from a 1.5-yard-deep slot)
    p.route("X", r.go(14)); p.route("Z", r.go(14)); p.route("H", r.out(9.0, 4)); p.route("Y", r.out(9.0, 4))
    for dk, ok in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y")):
        p.man(dk, ok)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.8, -4.0, 2.6)], "block")                      # six-man protection: the back stays in
    # the quarterback: drop, hold, then step up toward the left B gap
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.7, -7.0, 0.0), (1.5, -7.0, 0.0), (2.3, -4.0, -2.4)], "run")
    # the line: pass sets; the tackles are pushed back by the ends, the guards and center hold the inside
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.6, -2.0, -4.2), (1.8, -3.3, -4.8), (2.3, -3.6, -5.0)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.6, -1.8, -1.5), (2.3, -2.4, -1.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.6, -1.8, 0.3), (2.3, -2.2, 0.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.6, -1.8, 1.9), (2.3, -2.4, 2.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.6, -2.0, 4.2), (1.8, -3.3, 4.8), (2.3, -3.6, 5.0)], "block")
    # the rush: ends stay outside their tackles (contain), tackles push into the guards
    timed(p, "LDE", [(0.6, -0.8, -5.8), (1.8, -2.4, -6.2), (2.3, -2.8, -6.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDE", [(0.6, -0.8, 5.8), (1.8, -2.4, 6.2), (2.3, -2.8, 6.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.6, -0.6, -0.8), (2.3, -1.1, -0.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.6, -0.6, 2.3), (2.3, -1.1, 3.0)], "rush")
    # the spy: shuffles with the quarterback's shoulders, then starts to close
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.5, 6.0, 0.0), (2.0, 5.6, -0.8), (2.3, 4.9, -1.4)], "path")
    p.highlight("MIKE", color=PURPLE)
    return p


spy = spy_play()
T_SPY = 2.3
MEET = (2.1, -3.3)
fld = snapshot(spy, T_SPY, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.5, 18.5), ruler_fs=6.3)
ax = fld.ax
PPs = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*spy.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
at = lambda k: tuple(float(v) for v in spy.position(k, T_SPY))  # noqa: E731
# the next half-second: the quarterback's escape and the spy's angle, and where they meet
for key, end, col, lw in (("QB", (MEET[0] - 0.5, MEET[1]), style.OFFENSE_DARK, 2.4),
                          ("MIKE", (MEET[0] + 0.4, MEET[1] + 0.2), PURPLE, 2.2)):
    x0, y0 = PPs(*at(key)); x1, y1 = PPs(*end)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=12, color=col, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=8, shrinkB=1,
                                 zorder=9))
xm, ym = PPs(*MEET)
ax.plot([float(xm)], [float(ym)], marker="x", ms=10, mew=2.6, color=style.INK, zorder=12)
point_to(fld, spy, (12.4, 6.6), at("MIKE"), "the spy (M): eyes on the\nQB, shuffling, now closing")
point_to(fld, spy, (1.8, -13.5), MEET, "spy meets him here:\n2 yards past the line,\nshort of the sticks", shrink=5)
point_to(fld, spy, (-7.6, 10.0), at("RDE"), "ends rush in their lanes,\noutside the tackles: contain")
point_to(fld, spy, (-7.6, -9.5), at("QB"), "quarterback steps up\ntoward the B gap")
point_to(fld, spy, (11.4, -9.2), at("LCB"), "man defenders run with their\nreceivers, backs to the quarterback")
plt.show()
```

The defense plays Cover 1, man coverage on every receiver who goes out, with one deep safety; it rushes four and assigns the Mike linebacker (purple ring) to the quarterback. The back has stayed in to block, so the Will who had him waits. The man defenders have turned and run with their receivers, backs to the quarterback.
