Who spies? Someone fast enough to match a running quarterback and big enough to tackle him: usually a
linebacker, sometimes a safety or nickel back against the fastest quarterbacks, occasionally a defensive
lineman who "rushes" by stepping up and sitting in the middle. A linebacker assigned to the back can also
be a *green dog* (some staffs say *hug* or *add-on*), who joins the rush only if the back stays in to
block ([Linebackers and the Second Level](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)).
The spy comes with a rush plan too: against a running quarterback the rushers play a
[mush rush](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mush-rush) (some say *cage rush*), staying square in their
[rush lanes](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rush-lane) and pushing the blockers back into the quarterback
instead of racing around them ([The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd)). The ends keep
[contain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contain), the pocket shrinks around him but doesn't open, and the
spy is the last line if he finds a crease anyway.

The trade is the familiar one: the spy is a defender who isn't covering anyone. In Cover 1 he usually
replaces the robber, so the middle of the field loses its best in-cut defender; in zone he is one fewer
underneath player. A spy can also be *used*. Offenses run a receiver right at him to make him choose, or
send the back on a route he has to respect, and a linebacker spying a quarterback who is faster than he is
can be outrun to the sideline. Like every third-down call, it works best as one of several from the same look.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: two spies for Lamar Jackson, 2024 and 2025"}
Lamar Jackson, the most dangerous running quarterback of his era, sees spies as often as anyone, and two
games a year apart show both sides of the bargain.

**Chiefs 2024, opening night (September 5).** Kansas City moved linebacker Leo Chenal all over its front
(in the box, on the defensive line and over the slot) and used him to spy Jackson in key moments,
mirroring him and running him down on scrambles.[^chenal] It didn't
stop the running: Jackson carried 16 times for 122 yards, including
10 scrambles, and on third down he ran 5 times for
39 yards and 3 conversions. The Chiefs won anyway,
27–20, in a game decided on its final snap.

**Lions 2025, Week 3 (September 22, *Monday Night Football*).** Detroit's coordinator Kelvin Sheppard,
who had earlier said publicly that he didn't like using a spy, built a plan around one and made it hard to find. Jackson ran
7 times for 35 yards, was sacked 7 times,
and the Lions won in Baltimore, 38–30. Sheppard gave the credit not
to the spy but to the disguise around it: "it's because we're making everything look the same," he said,
"and when you do that, it's impossible to know who's coming, who's the spy, who's in coverage."[^sheppard]

**What to notice:** before a third-and-medium snap against a running quarterback, look for the linebacker
who sits straight in front of him at 5 or 6 yards and doesn't move with any receiver. After the snap,
watch him: a spy shuffles with the quarterback's shoulders. A green-dog rusher who comes forward late is
the same idea, disguised.
:::

## The third-down dial at a glance

Put the chapter's pieces side by side. The distance sets the menu for both sides; the pre-snap picture
tells you which item is likely, but only some calls have a reliable tell, because the defense works hard
to make the rest look alike.

| Distance | Offense's usual tools | Defense's usual calls | What you can see before the snap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short (1–3) | Power run, sneak, quick man-beaters (slant, rub) | Tight man (Cover 1), Cover 0, a packed box | No deep safety, pressed corners, linebackers mugged in the A gaps: Cover 0 or a disguise of it |
| Medium (4–6) | Option routes, mesh, rubs, matchups, empty | Cover 1 with a robber, mugs and disguise, some pressure | One deep safety, defenders tight on receivers; the robber or a mug shows where help is |
| Long (7–10) | Sticks routes past the line, six-man protection, hot throws | Blitz and simulated pressure, 2-Man, sticks zone | Dime personnel; defenders walked up to the line (blitz *or* sim: you usually can't tell which); two deep with tight, inside defenders suggests 2-Man |
| Very long (11+) | Screen, draw, safe completion, a shot | Sticks zone, rush three/drop eight | Six or more defensive backs, soft corners, two or three deep; only three linemen with a hand down hints at rush three |
| Any distance, running QB | Scramble, designed run, routes at the spy | Spy, mush rush | A linebacker in front of the quarterback at 5–7 yards, lined up on nobody |

## Is third down a skill?

Third down feels like the purest test of a team, and it is a big one. But it is also a small sample: a
team faces roughly 200 to 230 third downs a season, and every one is a coin weighted by distance. Two
consequences are worth knowing.

First, **early downs decide a lot of third down.** A team that is on schedule faces third-and-3, not
third-and-9, and converts more often without being any better *at* third down. How do we know? With a
**correlation**, a number between 0 and 1 (for this kind of comparison) that measures how well one
season's figure lines up with the next: 0 means last year tells you nothing about this year, 1 means it
tells you everything, and anything around 0.2 or 0.3 is a weak link, real but swamped by luck. Across
2016–2025, a team's success rate on first and second down predicted its third-down conversion rate the
*next* season (correlation 0\.33) nearly as well as its own third-down rate did
(0\.39).[^stab] Neither is strong, and the early-down number, which comes from about four
times as many plays, does almost as well.

Second, **defensive third-down numbers are noisy.** A defense's third-down conversion rate allowed
carried over from one season to the next with a correlation of only 0\.20: barely more
than nothing. A defense
that "gets off the field" one year often doesn't the next, which is a reason to judge third-down defenses
on what they do (pressure, coverage, tackling) more than on the conversion rate alone. Offenses are more
stable, but the gap between the best and worst is still modest: in 2025 the best offense converted
51% of its third downs, the worst 32%.

None of that makes third down unimportant; it makes it *consequential and noisy at once*, which is
exactly what you'd expect of a single high-stakes snap. [Expected Points, EPA, and Success
Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd) has the tools to measure it.

## Film room: the Patriots' option routes

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots 2009–2019 — Welker, Edelman and the sticks"}
The Patriots of the Tom Brady era built much of their third-down offense on slot receivers running option
routes set just past the sticks ([Passing Game Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)
and [The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd) introduce the route and Wes Welker). The
data shows what that meant on third down.

- **Wes Welker, 2009–2012.** Welker was New England's most-targeted receiver on third down in
  4 of those 4 seasons and the target on 28% of Brady's
  third-down throws to a named receiver. Those throws converted 48% of the time,
  against 39% for third-down targets across the league. And the typical Welker target
  was thrown **exactly to the line to gain**: the median distance between the throw's depth and the sticks
  was 0 yards. That looks like a contradiction: throws aimed right at the line are
the chart's weak spot. Welker beat the dip for the two reasons the dip exists. It comes from balls thrown
*into* a defender sitting at the sticks; the option route against zone finds the gap *between* two of them
and sits down in it, facing the quarterback. And it comes from defenders who have time to close; Brady
threw as Welker settled, before anyone could. Caught on the line with nobody in front of him, a receiver
only has to turn and fall forward.
- **Julian Edelman, 2013, 2016 and 2019** (the three seasons in which he played all 16 games; he missed 2017 injured):
  26% of third-down targets, converting 45% against a league
  41%.[^pats2]

Why did it work? Because the option route attacks the defense's third-down plan at its core. Against man
coverage the slot defender has to choose a side, and the receiver breaks the other way; against zone the
receiver sits down in the gap at the sticks, facing the quarterback. Brady could throw before the break was
finished, because he and his receiver read the same defender. **What to notice** on old Patriots third
downs: the slot receiver's first few steps are the same every time; the break comes at the sticks; the ball
is in the air before he turns.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Past the sticks?** On every third down for one half, make a prediction before the snap and check it
after.

- **Say the bucket out loud:** short (1–3), medium (4–6), long (7–10) or very long (11+). Then make the
  base-rate call: short, run or quick pass; medium, quick man-beater; long, a route past the sticks against
  pressure; very long, a safe completion or a draw.
- **Read the offense.** Did the best receiver move to the slot? Is the back still in the backfield (likely
  to stay in and block a blitzer) or did the offense go empty (five out, and the quarterback has to beat any
  extra rusher himself)?
- **Read the package.** How many defensive backs came on? Did a big tackle leave for a pass rusher? How many
  defenders are within five yards of the line, and how many deep? No deep safety means Cover 0; three or four
  deep with linemen standing up means the defense may drop eight. Then watch the quarterback point and shout:
  he is setting the protection's count, and the defense is trying to make that count wrong.
- **Find a spy.** Against a running quarterback, look for a linebacker or safety sitting in front of him
  who isn't lined up on any receiver.
- **Predict the target: past the line, or short of it?** Then, after the play, note where the ball was
  caught relative to the orange line, and who made the tackle.
- **For your log:** for each third down, write the bucket, your prediction (past or short), what happened,
  and the number of rushers. Over a game you'll see the defense's third-down personality (pressure,
  sticks, or both) and whether the offense's targets live past the line or short of it.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: third-and-3 at midfield"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-zero .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dfn = four_down(ldt=-2.75, rdt=2.75) + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, -1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, 1.0, "W"),
    D("NB", "NB", 0.9, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -3.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 0.9, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 0.9, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=55, to_go=3)
p.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 11.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, upto=10)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Third-and-3 near midfield. The offense is in 11 personnel, 2x2, with the back beside the quarterback. The defense has the Mike (M) and Will (W) standing in the A gaps, the nickel ($) pressed on H, both corners pressed, and both safeties (green rings) walked down to 6 or 7 yards.](10-02-third-down_files/figure-html/fig-predict-zero-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-zero}
:::
:::


**What is the defense likely to do, and what should the offense want to have called?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A Cover 0 blitz is the likeliest reading: man on every receiver, nobody deep, six or more rushing.**
Count the deep players: none. Both corners and the nickel are pressed, which usually means man coverage.
With the two linebackers mugged in the A gaps and both safeties walked down, the defense has up to eight
possible rushers and no one to protect against a long completion. That only makes sense on a
short-yardage down, which is where the league calls Cover 0 most (the Cover 0 section has the rates). It
could still be a disguise: one safety may bail at the snap into a Cover 1, and one of the mugged linebackers
may drop.

**What the offense wants** is a quick throw that beats tight man coverage before the rush arrives: a slant
from X or Z against an outside-leverage corner, a rub between H and the back, or a quick out. A run is live
only if the offense can account for the mugged linebackers, with a blocker for each of them, and against
this look the quick throw is the better bet. Even the quarterback sneak runs straight into the two
linebackers standing in its gaps; it becomes a better call once one of them shows he is dropping. What the
offense should *not* have called is a slow-developing route past the sticks: on third-and-3 it doesn't need
one, and against six rushers it won't get time.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: third-and-13 from the 20"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-drop .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dfn = four_down() + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.5, 0.8, "M"),
    D("NB", "NB", 7.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 7.0, 9.5, "D"), D("SS", "SS", 15.5, 9.0, "SS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 15.5, -9.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=30, to_go=13)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 18.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Third-and-13 from the offense's own 20. The defense has four linemen down (E, T, T, E), one linebacker (M) at 7.5 yards, and six defensive backs: the nickel ($) and the dime back (D) 7 yards off the slots, the corners 8 off, and two safeties 15 to 16 yards deep, one on each half of the field.](10-02-third-down_files/figure-html/fig-predict-drop-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-drop}
:::
:::


**How many will rush, where will the coverage sit, and what would you call if you were the offense?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely four rushers, with a two-deep coverage behind them and everything underneath sinking to
the sticks.** This is the third-and-very-long package: dime personnel, two safeties deep, corners off, and
only one linebacker. At 11 or more yards, defenses rushed exactly four on about
76% of charted dropbacks in 2023–2025, so
the base call is four. Behind it, two safeties high usually means a two-deep zone (Cover 2 or quarters)
or 2-Man. Either way, expect the underneath defenders to drop to 12 or 13 yards, so that every route that
converts runs into a defender and every route that's open is short. Two catches: a simulated pressure
looks exactly like this until the snap (an end drops, the Mike or a defensive back rushes), and an end who
drops turns it into rush three. The picture tells you the distance-based call, not the exact one.

**The offense's options** are the third-and-long menu. If it wants the first down, the soft spot of a
two-deep shell is the middle of the field between and under the safeties, 14 to 18 yards deep: a dig or a
seam, thrown on time. If it wants the possession, the draw and the screen are built for this picture: a
light box, one linebacker who will drop, rushers chasing upfield. From its own 20, a 9-yard draw that sets
up a punt from the 29 is a reasonable outcome, and an interception at the 35 is the disaster to avoid.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-5 against a quarterback who runs"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-spy .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dfn = four_down(lde=-6.4, rde=6.4) + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.2, 0.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.7, -3.2, "W"),
    D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, 8.6, "SS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=60, to_go=5)
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 16.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, upto=15)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Third-and-5 at midfield; the quarterback is one of the league's best runners. The defense presses the corners and walks the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS) up on the slots, with one deep safety (FS). Four linemen are down, the Will (W) is at about 4 yards over the back, and the Mike (M, green ring) stands 6 yards deep, directly in front of the quarterback, lined up on no one.](10-02-third-down_files/figure-html/fig-predict-spy-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-spy}
:::
:::


**What is the Mike's job, what coverage is behind him, and where is the offense's best throw?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The Mike is probably a spy, in Cover 1.** Every receiver has a defender pressed or tight on him (the
corners on X and Z, the nickel on H, the safety on Y, the Will on the back), one safety is deep, and the
Mike is lined up on nobody, square to the quarterback at spy depth. Against a quarterback who runs on
third-and-5, the defense has given up its robber to keep him in the pocket.

**Where to throw:** not right in front of the spy. His eyes are on the quarterback, so he sees every throw
that crosses his face at 5 to 8 yards, and spies rob those throws all the time. The good throws are the
ones he can't get to:

- **Behind him and in front of the free safety:** a dig or an over route at 10 to 14 yards. In Cover 1 with
  no robber, that is the space the defense emptied, and the spy can't turn and run back to it while
  watching the quarterback.
- **Away from leverage, outside:** an out or option-out by a slot receiver whose defender is aligned inside
  him, toward the sideline the spy can't reach.
- **Make the spy choose:** send the back on a route right at him, or a receiver across his face, so that
  covering the route means leaving the quarterback.

And the quarterback still has his legs: a spy who is slower than him has to be right about the angle.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Third down decides drives**, about three points of expected value on one snap, and the league converts
  about two in five, every year. The distance is the whole story: short third downs are converted most of
  the time, very long ones rarely.
- **The distance is information, so both sides specialise.** Defenses add defensive backs and pass rushers
  as the distance grows; offenses set their routes by the line to gain, put their best receiver where he can
  win, count the protection, and keep a third-down back.
- **Aim a yard or two past the sticks.** Third-down throws aimed there convert most often; throws short of
  the line rarely do, except on third-and-short, in four-down territory, or when the yards after the catch
  are the plan. Option routes, rubs and mesh exist to win that yard against man coverage, which costs the
  defense flags as well as catches.
- **The defense picks a point on a dial:** Cover 0 and tight man on short yardage, pressure (real and
  simulated) and 2-Man on third-and-7 to 10, sticks defense and rush three/drop eight on very long, and a spy
  when the quarterback can run. Each call gives something up, none wins on average once the distance is held
  still, and the best defenses show the same look for all of them.
- **Third-and-long is often about the possession, not the down.** Screens and draws rarely convert, but
  they avoid disasters, shorten punts, and keep the rush honest for the next one.
- **Third down is consequential and noisy.** Early-down success predicts it nearly as well as past
  third-down success does, and defensive third-down rates barely carry over year to year.

Both teams also played Cover 0 more often on short third downs than on long ones.

[^scramble]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2021–2025 regular seasons: third-down dropbacks with `qb_scramble`, and the conversion rate of scrambles and of all dropbacks on third-and-7 to 10 (conversion as defined above).
